# FalkorDB vs PostgreSQL: the same investigation questions on the same book

Book: graph `claimgraph_scale`, 20001 claims, 72557 claim links and 37055 claimant links, copied from FalkorDB into PostgreSQL 18.6 (indexed tables, copy took 8.002s). Both run in local Docker on the same machine (WSL2), default settings except the query tuning below. Wall-clock times from Go, after a warm-up. Synthetic data; the numbers describe this book on this machine only. PostgreSQL statement timeout 10000 ms. Generated by `go run ./cmd/benchrel`.

Both sides apply the same rules: context-only identifiers never connect claims, weak identifiers used by more than 20 claims are infrastructure, identifiers with more than 100 links are not expanded beyond the first hop, the same claimant filing twice is no claim-level link, and every claim on a path is distinct. Every answer is compared before any time is reported.

Both engines returned **identical answers on every comparison** (details below), so every timing compares equivalent implementations of the same question.

## 1. Where the graph database excels: finding rings and evidence chains across the whole book

| question | FalkorDB (median ms) | PostgreSQL (median ms) | faster |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 every ring in the book | 84.6 | 3404.7 | **FalkorDB 40x** |
| Q4 strongest evidence chain at any depth | 7.0 | 195.3 | **FalkorDB 28x** |

These are the questions ClaimGraph's ring detection is built on. Listing every ring in the book (2998 rings) is one `CALL algo.WCC` in FalkorDB; plain PostgreSQL has no connected-components operator and needed 35 rounds of full-table label propagation. The strongest evidence chain between two claims at any depth is one `algo.SPpaths` call; in PostgreSQL it is an iterative Bellman-Ford over the same evidence costs. (Extensions such as pgRouting add graph algorithms to PostgreSQL; we compared plain PostgreSQL.)

## 2. Short lookups from one claim: tuned PostgreSQL is faster

| question | FalkorDB (median ms) | PostgreSQL (median ms) | faster |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1a hops=1 | 24.4 | 1.6 | PostgreSQL 15x |
| Q1a hops=2 | 49.4 | 2.2 | PostgreSQL 22x |
| Q1a hops=3 | 129.1 | 5.4 | PostgreSQL 24x |
| Q1b hops=1 | 26.8 | 1.6 | PostgreSQL 17x |
| Q1b hops=2 | 56.7 | 2.2 | PostgreSQL 26x |
| Q1b hops=3 | 150.0 | 5.8 | PostgreSQL 26x |
| Q2 ring | 7.5 | 1.1 | PostgreSQL 7x |

Both engines answer these in well under a second, fast enough for interactive investigation, but this is not a tie: on this book a tuned PostgreSQL wins. A 1-3 hop walk over 20,000 claims is a handful of B-tree index lookups. Two things to know when reading it:

- **PostgreSQL needed graph-specific engineering to get there.** Written the obvious way, the same 3-hop question took about 650 ms because the planner joined every transition in the book on every hop; it also needed the traversal rules hand-encoded as a view and a planner hint (see Tuning).
- **FalkorDB's time here is query execution, not the network** (the client round trip is about 0.5 ms): our traversal runs one Cypher pattern branch per evidence type and path shape, written for correctness and scale limits (fan-out guard, row caps), not micro-tuned per branch.

## What this means

- **Use the graph for what only a graph does well.** Ring detection over the whole book (FalkorDB 40x) and any-depth evidence chains (FalkorDB 28x) take one built-in call each in FalkorDB, and they are the core of ClaimGraph's ring story.
- **Do not claim speed for short lookups.** For bounded 1-3 hop questions from a single claim, a well-indexed relational database is faster on this book once tuned.
- **Same answers.** Both engines return the same connected claims, hop counts, ring members, ring list and path costs, so the comparison is between equivalent implementations, not between different questions.

Limits: one machine, one synthetic 20,000-claim book, PostgreSQL defaults plus the stated query tuning, FalkorDB defaults. Larger or denser books may change the picture in either direction.

Q1b evidence returned (all samples): Q1b hops=1 FalkorDB 1929 paths, PostgreSQL 1929 paths; Q1b hops=2 FalkorDB 5413 paths, PostgreSQL 8002 paths; Q1b hops=3 FalkorDB 8188 paths, PostgreSQL 17264 paths; FalkorDB keeps at most 5 example paths per claim beyond one hop (no evidence lost) and also returns evidence ids and timestamps; PostgreSQL returns every shortest path with the identifier on each step.

Q2 on FalkorDB serves rings from one algo.WCC result per evidence version: the first (cold) call took 1090 ms, the rest are above. PostgreSQL walks each ring with its own recursive query.

## Tuning applied to PostgreSQL

The recursive queries use `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (... OFFSET 0)` so each hop looks up only the claims on the frontier through the indexes. Without it the planner hash-joins the whole `step` view (every transition in the book) on every hop: one 3-hop question took about 650 ms of execution instead of about 1 ms. The strong-evidence adjacency is a precomputed, indexed table. Q3 and Q4 push only the nodes whose label or distance changed. Everything else is PostgreSQL 18 defaults.

## The PostgreSQL queries

```sql
-- the traversal rules
CREATE VIEW step AS
  SELECT a.claim_id AS src, b.claim_id AS dst, e.links AS deg, a.entity AS via
  FROM claim_entity a
  JOIN entity e ON e.entity = a.entity
  JOIN claim_entity b ON b.entity = a.entity AND b.rel = a.rel AND b.claim_id <> a.claim_id
  JOIN claim ca ON ca.claim_id = a.claim_id
  JOIN claim cb ON cb.claim_id = b.claim_id
  WHERE ca.claimant_id <> cb.claimant_id   -- the same person filing twice is no shared-entity link
    AND NOT e.context                      -- context-only identifiers never connect claims
    AND (e.strong OR e.links <= 20)        -- weak identifiers used by > 20 claims are infrastructure
  UNION ALL
  SELECT ca.claim_id, cb.claim_id, e.links, ka.entity
  FROM claim ca
  JOIN claimant_entity ka ON ka.claimant_id = ca.claimant_id
  JOIN entity e ON e.entity = ka.entity
  JOIN claimant_entity kb ON kb.entity = ka.entity AND kb.rel = ka.rel AND kb.claimant_id <> ka.claimant_id
  JOIN claim cb ON cb.claimant_id = kb.claimant_id
  WHERE cb.claim_id <> ca.claim_id;

-- Q1a
WITH RECURSIVE walk(claim, depth, path, maxdeg) AS (
  SELECT s.dst, 1, ARRAY[$1::text, s.dst], s.deg FROM step s WHERE s.src = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.dst, w.depth + 1, w.path || s.dst, GREATEST(w.maxdeg, s.deg)
  FROM walk w CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT st.dst, st.deg FROM step st WHERE st.src = w.claim OFFSET 0) s
  WHERE w.depth < $2 AND NOT s.dst = ANY(w.path) AND GREATEST(w.maxdeg, s.deg) <= 100
)
SELECT claim, min(depth) FROM walk GROUP BY claim

-- Q1b
WITH RECURSIVE walk(claim, depth, path, via, maxdeg) AS (
  SELECT s.dst, 1, ARRAY[$1::text, s.dst], ARRAY[s.via], s.deg FROM step s WHERE s.src = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.dst, w.depth + 1, w.path || s.dst, w.via || s.via, GREATEST(w.maxdeg, s.deg)
  FROM walk w CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT st.dst, st.deg, st.via FROM step st WHERE st.src = w.claim OFFSET 0) s
  WHERE w.depth < $2 AND NOT s.dst = ANY(w.path) AND GREATEST(w.maxdeg, s.deg) <= 100
)
SELECT claim, depth, path, via FROM (
  SELECT claim, depth, path, via, min(depth) OVER (PARTITION BY claim) AS best FROM walk
) x WHERE depth = best

-- strong-evidence adjacency (Q2-Q4)
CREATE TABLE strong_edge AS
  SELECT 'C:' || claim_id AS a, 'E:' || entity AS b, CASE category WHEN 'payout' THEN 4 ELSE 5 END AS w FROM claim_entity WHERE category IN ('payout','device')
  UNION ALL SELECT 'E:' || entity, 'C:' || claim_id, CASE category WHEN 'payout' THEN 4 ELSE 5 END FROM claim_entity WHERE category IN ('payout','device')
  UNION ALL SELECT 'C:' || claim_id, 'K:' || claimant_id, 0 FROM claim
  UNION ALL SELECT 'K:' || claimant_id, 'C:' || claim_id, 0 FROM claim
  UNION ALL SELECT 'K:' || claimant_id, 'E:' || entity, CASE category WHEN 'contact' THEN 8 ELSE 10 END FROM claimant_entity
  UNION ALL SELECT 'E:' || entity, 'K:' || claimant_id, CASE category WHEN 'contact' THEN 8 ELSE 10 END FROM claimant_entity;
CREATE INDEX ON strong_edge (a);
ANALYZE strong_edge;

-- Q2
WITH RECURSIVE comp(node) AS (
  SELECT 'C:' || $1::text
  UNION
  SELECT e.b FROM comp CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT se.b FROM strong_edge se WHERE se.a = comp.node OFFSET 0) e
)
SELECT substr(node, 3) FROM comp WHERE node LIKE 'C:%'

-- Q3 (repeated until nothing changes)
WITH cand AS (
  SELECT e.b AS node, min(l.comp) AS c
  FROM frontier f JOIN lbl l ON l.node = f.node JOIN strong_edge e ON e.a = f.node
  GROUP BY e.b
), upd AS (
  UPDATE lbl SET comp = cand.c FROM cand WHERE lbl.node = cand.node AND cand.c < lbl.comp RETURNING lbl.node
)
INSERT INTO nxt SELECT node FROM upd

-- Q4 (repeated until nothing changes)
WITH cand AS (
  SELECT e.b AS node, min(d.d + e.w) AS c
  FROM frontier f JOIN dist d ON d.node = f.node JOIN strong_edge e ON e.a = f.node
  GROUP BY e.b
), upd AS (
  INSERT INTO dist SELECT node, c FROM cand WHERE c <= 999
  ON CONFLICT (node) DO UPDATE SET d = EXCLUDED.d WHERE EXCLUDED.d < dist.d
  RETURNING node
)
INSERT INTO nxt SELECT node FROM upd
```

FalkorDB: Q1a/Q1b are built from the fixed Cypher fragments in `internal/investigate/traverse.go` (one staged MATCH per hop, one branch per path shape); Q2/Q3 call `algo.WCC` and Q4 calls `algo.SPpaths` (`internal/graphalgo`).
